drills.los_text: discuss roles of fixed-income securities in portfolios and how fixed-income mandates may be classified

questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely a role of fixed-income securities in a portfolio?

options.A: Regular cash flows.
options.B: Diversification benefits.
options.C: Guaranteed capital appreciation exceeding equities.

rationales.A: Regular cash flows are one of the identified roles. Scheduled coupon and principal payments let an investor match known future obligations, which is why fixed income anchors liability-relative portfolios.
rationales.B: Diversification is one of the identified roles. Fixed income has historically exhibited low correlation with other asset classes, notably equities, so adding it reduces portfolio return volatility.
rationales.C: Fixed-income securities offer no guaranteed capital appreciation, and certainly none exceeding equities. Their return comes mainly from coupon income and the return of principal, and prices fall when interest rates or spreads rise. The roles identified for fixed income are (1) diversification benefits, from low correlations with other asset classes, (2) regular cash flows, which allow investors to meet known future obligations, and (3) inflation-hedging potential, particularly through inflation-linked bonds and floating-rate coupons.

questions.stem: Within the fixed-income asset class, correlations between FI indexes are most likely driven by:

options.A: Dividend yields of the issuers' equities.
options.B: Credit rating alone.
options.C: The interest rate (duration) component and geography.

rationales.A: Dividend yield is an equity attribute and does not drive correlations among fixed-income indexes. Those correlations trace to the shared interest rate exposure of the underlying bonds, that is their duration, and to geography.
rationales.B: Rating matters at the security level, and it is why below-investment-grade indexes behave differently from investment-grade ones, but index-level correlations are driven largely by shared duration exposure and by regional interest rate linkages rather than by rating on its own.
rationales.C: Within the fixed-income asset class, correlations between indexes are driven largely by the interest rate component, that is duration, and by geography. In developed economies, investment-grade securities with a low probability of default are highly correlated with interest rate changes in the sovereign yield curve. Below-investment-grade securities are affected more by changes in spread than by changes in the general level of interest rates and often exhibit stronger correlations with equity markets. Correlations between interest rates and spreads can often be negative.

questions.stem: During periods of market stress, a flight to quality most likely results in:

options.A: Increased correlation between government bonds and equities.
options.B: Unchanged correlation between government bonds and equities.
options.C: Decreased correlation between government bonds and equities.

rationales.A: This is the opposite pattern. In a flight to quality, government bond prices rise while equity prices fall, which pushes the correlation between the two down rather than up.
rationales.B: Correlations shift materially in a crisis rather than holding steady. A flight to quality is precisely the episode in which the historical correlation structure breaks down, which is why stress-period correlations are modeled separately from long-run averages.
rationales.C: During periods of market stress, investors exhibit a flight to quality by buying safer assets such as government bonds, increasing their prices, and selling riskier assets such as equity securities and high-yield bonds, lowering their prices. These actions may decrease the correlation between government bonds and equity securities, as well as between government bonds and high-yield bonds. At the same time, the correlation between riskier assets such as equity securities and high-yield bonds may increase.

questions.stem: Over the 20 years through December 2019, the correlations of the S&P 500 with US corporate high yield and with the 10-year US Treasury are closest to:

options.A: High yield -0.30 and 10-year Treasury 0.63.
options.B: High yield 0.63 and 10-year Treasury -0.30.
options.C: High yield 0.20 and 10-year Treasury 0.02.

rationales.A: These two values are swapped. Approximately -0.30 is the 10-year US Treasury's correlation with the S&P 500 and 0.63 is US corporate high yield's. High yield carries equity-like risk, hence a high positive correlation with equities, while Treasuries diversify equity risk, hence a negative correlation.
rationales.B: Over the 20-year period through December 2019, S&P 500 correlations were approximately: US Aggregate -0.09, 10-year US Treasury -0.30, US Corporate 0.20, Global Aggregate 0.15, US TIPS 0.02, US Corporate High Yield 0.63, and emerging market (USD) 0.51. High yield's 0.63 reflects its equity-like risk profile, while the 10-year Treasury's -0.30 reflects its role as a diversifier of equity risk.
rationales.C: Approximately 0.20 is the US Corporate (investment-grade) correlation and 0.02 is US TIPS. Neither figure belongs to high yield or to the 10-year Treasury, and both understate how equity-like high yield is while missing the Treasury's negative correlation with equities.

questions.stem: Relative to conventional bonds, inflation-linked bonds are most likely to:

options.A: Adjust principal for inflation.
options.B: Leave principal unadjusted for inflation.
options.C: Eliminate inflation risk in all market conditions.

rationales.A: Inflation-linked bonds pay a return directly linked to an index of consumer prices and adjust the principal for inflation, so the return comprises a real return plus a component tied directly to the inflation rate. All else equal, they typically exhibit lower return volatility than conventional bonds and equities, because that volatility depends on real rather than nominal interest rates, and real rate volatility is typically lower than nominal rate volatility.
rationales.B: Leaving principal unadjusted describes a floating-rate coupon instrument. Resetting the coupon protects interest income as rates and inflation rise, but the principal is not indexed, so the real value of the redemption amount is still eroded by inflation.
rationales.C: Inflation risk is not eliminated in all market conditions. Principal and coupon are indexed to realized consumer price inflation, but the real yield still fluctuates, so prices move with real rates, and the price index used may also differ from an individual investor's own inflation experience.

questions.stem: The two broad categories of fixed-income mandates are most likely:

options.A: Government and corporate.
options.B: Liability-based and total return.
options.C: Domestic and international.

rationales.A: Government and corporate describe issuer types, not the two broad categories into which fixed-income mandates are divided.
rationales.B: Fixed-income mandates split into two broad categories. Liability-based mandates — cash flow matching, duration matching, contingent immunization, and hybrid approaches — are collectively the asset/liability management (ALM) or liability-driven investing (LDI) approaches, in which the portfolio is structured against a specific set of liabilities. Total return mandates — pure indexing, enhanced indexing, and active management — are structured against a benchmark index rather than against liabilities.
rationales.C: Domestic and international describe geographic categories, not the two broad categories into which fixed-income mandates are divided.

questions.stem: A total return mandate is least likely to be implemented through:

options.A: Contingent immunization.
options.B: Pure indexing.
options.C: Enhanced indexing.

rationales.A: Contingent immunization is a liability-based mandate, not a total return mandate. It is a hybrid approach that combines immunization with an active management approach when assets exceed the present value of the liabilities, so the surplus can be managed actively while the liability remains covered. The three total return approaches are pure indexing (full replication), enhanced indexing, and active management.
rationales.B: Pure indexing, or full replication, is one of the three total return approaches; both its targeted active return and its targeted active risk are zero.
rationales.C: Enhanced indexing is one of the three total return approaches. It maintains a close link to the benchmark, permitting only small deviations from benchmark weights and tracking the primary risk factor exposures — particularly duration — very closely, while seeking modest outperformance.

questions.stem: Enhanced indexing is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Outperformance of 0 bps with no deviation from benchmark weights.
options.B: Outperformance of 20–30 bps with small deviations from benchmark weights.
options.C: Outperformance of 50 bps or more with large deviations from benchmark weights.

rationales.A: Matching the benchmark in every dimension — holding all constituents at exact index weights with zero deviation, and so targeting no active return at all — is pure indexing. Enhanced indexing permits small deviations from benchmark weights precisely in order to seek modest outperformance, so it is not a full-replication approach.
rationales.B: The enhanced indexing objective is modest outperformance of the benchmark, generally 20–30 bps, while active risk is kept low, typically around 50 bps or lower. Portfolio weights show small deviations from the underlying benchmark, and most primary risk factors are closely matched, particularly duration. Turnover is slightly higher than the underlying benchmark's. Enhanced indexing therefore sits between pure indexing, which targets zero active return and zero active risk, and active management, which targets 50 bps or more of outperformance with considerably larger deviations.
rationales.C: Large risk factor deviations and a target of 50 bps or more of outperformance describe active management, not enhanced indexing, which targets roughly 20–30 bps of outperformance while holding active risk near 50 bps or lower and matching primary risk factors closely.

questions.stem: Compared with indexing approaches, active fixed-income management is most likely characterized by:

options.A: Higher targeted outperformance and higher active risk.
options.B: Minimal deviation from the benchmark on any characteristic.
options.C: The same return objective as pure indexing.

rationales.A: Active management targets higher outperformance of the benchmark, generally around 50 bps or more, and accepts higher levels of active risk. Portfolio weights show significant deviations from the underlying benchmark, and the target risk factor profile carries large risk factor deviations from the benchmark, particularly in duration, although some active strategies instead concentrate idiosyncratic risk. Turnover is considerably higher than the underlying benchmark's turnover, and active managers normally charge higher management fees than pure or enhanced indexing managers.
rationales.B: Minimal deviation from the benchmark on every characteristic describes pure indexing, which replicates the benchmark rather than deviating from it in order to earn an active return.
rationales.C: Pure indexing targets an active return and an active risk of zero. Active management has a different objective: outperformance of roughly 50 bps or more, accepting the higher active risk that comes with it.

drills.los_text: describe fixed-income portfolio measures of risk and return as well as correlation characteristics

questions.stem: Macaulay duration is most likely:

options.A: The price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve.
options.B: A weighted average of the time to receipt of the bond's promised payments.
options.C: A weighted average time to receipt divided by one plus the yield per period.

rationales.A: Price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve is effective duration, not Macaulay duration.
rationales.B: Macaulay duration (MacDur) is a weighted average of the time to receipt of the bond's promised payments, where the weights are the shares of the full price that correspond to each of the bond's promised future payments. It is therefore expressed in time units. Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield per period.
rationales.C: Dividing a weighted average time to receipt by one plus the yield per period gives modified duration. Macaulay duration is the weighted average itself, before that division.

questions.stem: Effective duration differs from modified duration most likely because effective duration:

options.A: cannot be computed for bonds with embedded options.
options.B: measures price sensitivity to a shift in the benchmark yield curve.
options.C: ignores yield changes and measures only the passage of time.

rationales.A: The opposite is true: effective duration is essential precisely for bonds whose cash flows change with rates, such as callable and putable bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It is modified duration that breaks down for those bonds, because it assumes the promised cash flows are fixed.
rationales.B: Effective duration is the sensitivity of a bond's price to a change in a benchmark yield curve — that is, to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve, ΔCurve. It is essential to measuring the interest rate risk of a complex bond where future cash flows are uncertain, such as a callable or putable bond or an MBS with embedded options, since those cash flows respond to the level of rates. EffDur = [(PV−) − (PV+)] / [2 × ΔCurve × PV0].
rationales.C: Effective duration measures the price response to a shift in the benchmark yield curve, so a yield change is its very input rather than something it ignores. Duration is expressed in time units, but it is not a measure of the passage of time.

questions.stem: Key rate duration, also called partial duration, most likely measures sensitivity to:

options.A: a change in the benchmark yield curve at a specific maturity segment.
options.B: a change in the bond's yield spread.
options.C: a change across all points on the benchmark yield curve.

rationales.A: Key rate duration (KeyRatDur), also called partial duration, measures a bond's sensitivity to a change in the benchmark yield curve at a specific maturity point or segment. Key rate durations help identify shaping risk for a bond or portfolio — that is, its sensitivity to changes in the shape of the benchmark yield curve, such as the curve becoming steeper or flatter or showing more or less curvature.
rationales.B: Sensitivity to a change in the yield spread is measured by spread duration, not by key rate duration, which works off the benchmark curve.
rationales.C: Sensitivity to a change across all points on the curve at once is measured by modified or effective duration. Key rate duration isolates a single maturity point or segment, which is what makes it useful for shaping risk.

questions.stem: Money duration, called dollar duration in the United States, is most likely:

options.A: The yield spread over government bonds.
options.B: The price change expressed in the bond's currency of denomination.
options.C: A measure of interest rate volatility.

rationales.A: A yield spread over government bonds is a spread measure, not a duration measure. Money duration expresses a price change in currency units.
rationales.B: Money duration is a measure of the price change in units of the currency in which the bond is denominated. It can be stated per 100 of par value or in terms of the bond's actual position size in the portfolio, and in the United States it is commonly called dollar duration. A related statistic is PVBP (price value of a basis point) — the change in price for a 1 bp change in yield, sometimes called DV01.
rationales.C: Interest rate volatility is an input to option and risk models, not what money duration measures. Money duration expresses a price change in currency units.

questions.stem: The price value of a basis point (PVBP) is most likely related to money duration in that PVBP:

options.A: scales money duration to the money gained or lost per basis point.
options.B: rescales money duration into a percentage of par rather than a currency amount.
options.C: bears no relationship to money duration.

rationales.A: PVBP is an estimate of the change in a bond's price given a 1 bp change in yield to maturity. It scales money duration so that it can be interpreted as money gained or lost for each basis point change in the reference interest rate. In North America it is also referred to as the dollar value of an 0.01, or DV01, calibrated to a bond's par value of 100. The related statistic basis point value is BPV = money duration × 0.0001. The terms PVBP and DV01 are used interchangeably.
rationales.B: The scaling is by 0.0001, one basis point, which turns money duration into a currency amount gained or lost per basis point. It is not a multiplication by 100, and it does not convert money duration into a percentage-of-par measure; money duration is already a currency figure.
rationales.C: PVBP is scaled money duration — the money gained or lost for each one-basis-point change in the reference rate — so the two measures are directly related, differing only by the 0.0001 scaling.

questions.stem: For option-free zero-coupon bonds, it is most likely that:

options.A: duration rises linearly with maturity and convexity rises with the square of duration.
options.B: duration rises linearly with maturity and convexity falls as duration rises.
options.C: duration falls as maturity lengthens and convexity is unrelated to duration.

rationales.A: Two useful heuristics apply to zero-coupon (option-free) bonds. First, Macaulay durations increase linearly with maturity, so a 30-year zero has three times the duration of a 10-year zero. Second, convexity is approximately proportional to duration squared, so a 30-year zero has about nine times (3²) the convexity of a 10-year zero. Related to these: coupon-paying bonds have more convexity than zero-coupon bonds of the same duration — a 30-year coupon-paying bond with duration of roughly 18 years has more convexity than an 18-year zero — and a zero-coupon bond has the lowest convexity of all bonds of a given duration.
rationales.B: The relationship is direct, not inverse. Convexity is approximately proportional to duration squared, so a longer-duration zero carries more convexity, not systematically less: a 30-year zero has about nine times the convexity of a 10-year zero.
rationales.C: Macaulay duration increases with maturity for zeros, and does so linearly — a 30-year zero has three times the duration of a 10-year zero. Convexity is not unrelated to duration either; it is approximately proportional to duration squared.

questions.stem: Spread duration is most likely defined as:

options.A: A measure of sensitivity to benchmark yield changes.
options.B: A measure of sensitivity to credit spread changes.
options.C: A measure of the yield curve's slope.

rationales.A: This describes modified or effective duration, which gives the approximate percentage price change for a 1% change in the bond's benchmark yield rather than in its credit spread. Spread duration isolates the spread component of that yield.
rationales.B: Spread duration is the measure used to determine a portfolio's sensitivity to changes in credit spreads. Duration indicates the percentage price effect of an interest rate change; spread duration measures the effect of a change in yield spread on a bond's price. It provides the approximate percentage increase (decrease) in bond price expected for a 1% decrease (increase) in credit spread.
rationales.C: The slope of the yield curve is a term structure measure describing the shape of the curve across maturities. Spread duration is a price-sensitivity measure for one bond or portfolio and says nothing about curve shape.

questions.stem: Compared with spread duration, duration times spread (DTS) is most likely designed to:

options.A: Remove the effect of duration from the credit risk measure.
options.B: Measure interest rate risk rather than credit risk.
options.C: Reflect spread changes as proportional rather than absolute.

rationales.A: DTS builds on duration rather than removing it. It scales spread duration by a factor equal to the current credit spread, so duration remains embedded in the measure; nothing about the credit risk measure becomes duration-free.
rationales.B: DTS is a credit risk measure, not a pure interest rate risk measure. Its whole purpose is to reflect how credit spreads behave — spread changes tend to occur on a proportional (percentage) basis rather than an absolute basis — and it is used when adjusting credit exposure, not when adjusting benchmark yield exposure.
rationales.C: DTS modifies the spread duration definition to incorporate the empirical observation that spread changes across the credit spectrum tend to occur on a proportional percentage basis rather than being based on absolute basis point changes. The measure weights spread duration by a factor equal to the current credit spread, increasing the magnitude of expected price changes for a given change in spread. Portfolio managers often use DTS when adjusting credit exposure by rating, for example reducing A-rated names and increasing BBB-rated credits.

questions.stem: Portfolio dispersion is most likely defined as:

options.A: The weighted mean of the times to receipt of cash flows.
options.B: The standard deviation of periodic total returns.
options.C: The weighted variance of the times to receipt of cash flows.

rationales.A: The weighted mean of the times to receipt of cash flows is Macaulay duration. Dispersion is measured around that mean rather than being the mean itself.
rationales.B: Dispersion is a cash flow timing statistic, not a return volatility statistic. The standard deviation of periodic total returns describes realized return variability and says nothing about when a portfolio's payments arrive relative to its duration.
rationales.C: Portfolio dispersion captures the variance of the times to receipt of cash flows with respect to the duration. Whereas Macaulay duration is the weighted average of the times to receipt of cash flows, dispersion is the weighted variance, measuring the extent to which the payments are spread out around the duration. Convexity is affected by the dispersion of cash flows: higher cash flow dispersion leads to an increase in convexity. Dispersion is also used in measuring interest rate immunization for liabilities.

drills.los_text: describe bond market liquidity, including the differences among market sub-sectors, and discuss the effect of liquidity on fixed-income portfolio management

questions.stem: Compared with equities, fixed-income markets are most likely:

options.A: More liquid.
options.B: Equally liquid.
options.C: Less liquid.

rationales.A: This is the opposite of the actual relationship: equity markets are generally the more liquid of the two, not the less liquid.
rationales.B: There are structural liquidity differences between the two markets, so they are not equally liquid. Equities trade continuously on exchanges, while much of the bond market trades over the counter and infrequently.
rationales.C: Compared with equities, fixed-income markets are generally less liquid. Many bonds do not trade at all or trade only infrequently; there is a large number of distinct fixed-income securities per issuer (multiple bonds outstanding versus typically one class of common stock); and liquidity is higher for the bonds of large, high-quality issuers and lower for smaller or lower-credit issuers.

questions.stem: Four bonds are available: a recently issued on-the-run sovereign bond of a high-credit-quality government, a sovereign bond of the same government issued a year ago, a high-credit-quality corporate bond, and a low-credit-quality corporate bond. Their ordering from most to least liquid is most likely:

options.A: Low-quality corporate, high-quality corporate, seasoned sovereign, on-the-run sovereign.
options.B: On-the-run sovereign, seasoned sovereign, high-quality corporate, low-quality corporate.
options.C: All four equally liquid.

rationales.A: This is the actual ordering reversed. Low-credit-quality corporate bonds are the least liquid of the four, not the most, and the on-the-run sovereign is the most liquid, not the least.
rationales.B: From most to least liquid the ordering is: (1) the recently issued on-the-run sovereign bond of a high-credit-quality government, (2) the sovereign bond of that same high-credit-quality government issued a year ago, (3) the high-credit-quality corporate bond, and (4) the low-credit-quality corporate bond. On-the-run sovereigns benefit from recency, issue size, and credit quality; the seasoned sovereign loses the recency advantage as trading migrates to the current on-the-run issue; corporate bonds trade less often still, and low-credit-quality corporates least of all.
rationales.C: Liquidity varies substantially across fixed-income segments — by issuer type, credit quality, issue size, and time since issuance — so these four bonds are not equally liquid.

questions.stem: Pricing bonds accurately is challenging most likely because:

options.A: Recent transaction prices, especially for corporate bonds, are often unavailable.
options.B: Matrix pricing is prohibited for infrequently traded bonds.
options.C: Trade-reporting systems cover only government bond transactions.

rationales.A: Sources for pricing recent bond transactions, notably corporate bonds, are not always readily available. Because many bonds do not trade or trade only infrequently, using recent transaction prices to represent current value is not practical, and reliance on last traded prices that may be out of date could result in costly trading decisions. Systems such as TRACE in the United States and EMMA for US municipals increase transparency. Where recent prices are missing, matrix pricing uses observable liquid benchmark yields of similar maturity or duration together with the benchmark spreads of bonds of comparable time to maturity, credit quality, and sector to estimate a current market yield and price.
rationales.B: Matrix pricing is the standard solution for infrequently traded bonds, not a prohibited practice. It estimates a current market yield and price from observable liquid benchmark yields and the benchmark spreads of comparable bonds, so an infrequently traded bond can still be valued.
rationales.C: TRACE reports US corporate bond trades and EMMA covers US municipal bonds, so these systems increase corporate and municipal price transparency rather than excluding those trades. The pricing difficulty arises in markets and segments where no such reporting exists.

questions.stem: TRACE and EMMA are most likely:

options.A: European regulatory frameworks.
options.B: Risk models for credit exposure.
options.C: US trade-reporting systems.

rationales.A: Both are US systems: TRACE is operated by FINRA and EMMA by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board. Similar initiatives exist elsewhere for corporate bonds traded on market exchanges, but neither of these two is a European framework.
rationales.B: Neither estimates or measures credit exposure. They are transparency and reporting systems that publish executed trade information so that market participants can observe recent prices.
rationales.C: TRACE, FINRA's Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine, covers US corporate bonds, and EMMA, the MSRB's Electronic Municipal Market Access, covers US municipal bonds. Both are electronic systems that help increase transparency. Similar initiatives play a similar role elsewhere for corporate bonds traded on market exchanges. In most bond markets, however, the lack of transparency in corporate bond trading remains a challenge.

questions.stem: In bond portfolio construction, an important trade-off most likely exists between:

options.A: Coupon rate and issuance size.
options.B: Yield to maturity and liquidity.
options.C: Duration and convexity.

rationales.A: Coupon rate and issue size are bond characteristics rather than competing portfolio objectives. Issue size does influence liquidity, but the investor is not forced to give up one of these two to obtain the other.
rationales.B: Investors' liquidity preferences directly influence portfolio construction, and the important trade-off is between yield to maturity and liquidity. Illiquid bonds typically carry higher yields to maturity, so a buy-and-hold investor seeking higher returns will often prefer less liquid bonds with higher YTMs, while an investor who prefers greater liquidity sacrifices return and chooses more liquid bonds with lower YTMs. Some investors also restrict holdings to bonds within a certain maturity range, which reduces the need to sell positions to generate cash inflows.
rationales.C: Duration and convexity are both measures of a bond's price sensitivity to yield changes and generally move together for straight bonds. The relationship between them is bond mathematics, not a choice the investor trades off in constructing a portfolio.

questions.stem: Bid-ask spreads on bonds are most likely affected by:

options.A: Issue size only.
options.B: Riskiness, with riskier bonds having narrower spreads.
options.C: Riskiness, complexity, and creditworthiness.

rationales.A: Issue size and the number of outstanding issues do matter, through their effect on liquidity, but they are not the only determinants. Bond complexity, where embedded options widen spreads, and creditworthiness also drive the bid-ask spread, so spreads do not depend on issue size alone.
rationales.B: The direction is reversed. Dealers' aversion to holding riskier bonds leads to wider, not narrower, bid-ask spreads, because dealers must finance their inventories and be compensated for the risk of holding them.
rationales.C: Several factors determine the bid-ask spread. First, riskiness: riskier bonds often have higher bid-ask spreads because of dealers' aversion to holding them, since dealers must finance inventories and want to cover both costs and profit. Second, bond complexity: plain vanilla corporate bonds normally have lower spreads than corporate bonds with non-standard or complex features such as embedded options. Third, creditworthiness: bonds of large, high-credit-quality corporations with many outstanding issues are the most liquid among corporate bonds and so carry relatively low bid-ask spreads. Government bond spreads are the lowest of all.

questions.stem: The cost impact of a corporate bond quoted with a 10 bp bid-ask spread and 15-year duration is closest to:

rationales.A: The cost impact is the bid-ask spread multiplied by duration: 0.0010 x 15 x 100 = 1.50%. A manager who buys the bond at $100 would, when the position is priced (typically at the bid or the midpoint), carry it at $98.50, reducing total portfolio return. That is the price that would be realized if the bond were sold, holding other factors constant. Higher transaction costs reduce the benefits of active portfolio decisions and may decrease portfolio managers' willingness to trade; investors can mitigate them by participating in the primary, new-issue market.
rationales.B: This is the quoted spread itself, 10 bp or 0.10%, not the price impact. The spread must be scaled by the bond's duration to translate a yield-space quote into a percentage price effect.
rationales.C: This is too large by an order of magnitude. A 15.00% impact would require a bid-ask spread of 100 bp against a 15-year duration, not the 10 bp quoted.

questions.stem: Bond dealers quote bid-ask spreads on bonds they choose to carry in inventory. Those quoted spreads are most likely:

options.A: narrower for less liquid bonds, which dealers discount to clear inventory.
options.B: unaffected by dealer inventories, which are hedged immediately.
options.C: wider for less liquid bonds, which dealers finance and hold longer.

rationales.A: The relationship runs the other way. The longer a bond is expected to sit in inventory, the wider the quoted spread must be, because the dealer has to recover the cost of obtaining funding and of holding the position. Dealers do not quote narrower spreads on less liquid bonds in order to move them faster; if anything, some illiquid bonds carry no quotes at all, and bid quotes in particular may be absent.
rationales.B: Inventory dynamics are precisely what drive the quotes. Buy and sell orders do not arrive simultaneously, so a dealer must hold bonds and finance them, and financing and holding costs accumulate for as long as the position sits on the balance sheet. A dealer cannot hedge every position instantly and is not certain how long a bond will remain in inventory; the bid-ask spread is how those costs, plus a profit, are recovered.
rationales.C: Bond dealers often carry an inventory of bonds because buy and sell orders do not arrive simultaneously, and a dealer is not certain how long bonds will remain in inventory. Less liquid bonds are likely to remain in inventory longer than liquid bonds. A dealer provides bid-ask quotes on bonds of its choice, and some illiquid bonds will have no quotes, particularly bid quotes. Because dealers must finance their inventories, they incur costs in obtaining funding and in holding those bonds, and they cover those costs and earn a profit through the bid-ask spread. Spreads are therefore higher for illiquid bonds that are likely to remain in inventory longer.

drills.los_text: describe and interpret a model for fixed-income returns

questions.stem: The components of expected return on a fixed-income portfolio are most likely:

options.A: yield to maturity alone.
options.B: coupon income, rolldown return, yield and spread views, and currency effects.
options.C: coupon income and price change alone.

rationales.A: Yield to maturity is a single summary measure of a bond's promised return, not a decomposition of it. It identifies none of the separate sources of return: the rolldown along an unchanged curve, the price effects of the investor's views on benchmark yields and on yield spreads, or currency gains and losses on assets denominated in foreign currencies.
rationales.B: Expected fixed-income return decomposes into five components: (1) coupon income, the annual coupon divided by the current bond price; (2) rolldown return, the bond's percentage price change assuming an unchanged yield curve over the strategy horizon; (3) E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of benchmark yields to maturity and the term structure of yield volatility); (4) E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yield spreads); and (5) E(currency gains or losses on assets denominated in foreign currencies). The sum of coupon income and rolldown return is called the rolling yield. An equivalent presentation combines the two price-view terms into a single E(ΔPrice from the investor's views of yields and spreads) and subtracts E(credit losses), equal to the probability of default × loss severity, as an explicit component; in the five-part model above, expected credit losses are captured within the spread-view term.
rationales.C: Two components are inadequate. Coupon income paired with an undifferentiated price change does not separate rolldown return along an unchanged curve from the price changes driven by the investor's yield view and spread view, and it omits currency gains or losses on foreign-currency assets entirely.

questions.stem: The rolldown return is most likely:

options.A: The change in yield spread over the horizon.
options.B: The coupon interest received over the horizon.
options.C: The percentage price change assuming an unchanged yield curve.

rationales.A: A change in the yield spread drives the spread-view component of the decomposition, E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yield spreads), not the rolldown return. Rolldown holds the yield curve fixed and measures only the price effect of the bond aging along that unchanged curve.
rationales.B: Coupon interest received is coupon income, the annual coupon divided by the current bond price, not rolldown. The two are distinct components: coupon income plus rolldown return is what is called the rolling yield, so rolldown cannot be the coupon itself.
rationales.C: The rolldown return equals the bond's percentage price change assuming an unchanged yield curve over the strategy horizon, computed as (bond price end-of-horizon − bond price beginning-of-horizon) / bond price beginning-of-horizon. Bonds trading at a premium to par will experience capital losses during their remaining life, and bonds trading at a discount will experience capital gains, because price converges toward par as the bond rolls down an unchanged curve. Coupon income plus rolldown return gives the rolling yield.

questions.stem: An investor's expected bond price change based on a view of benchmark yields is most likely:

options.A: A positive modified duration term with no convexity adjustment.
options.B: A coupon rate scaled by the holding period.
options.C: A negative modified duration term plus a convexity adjustment.

rationales.A: Two things are wrong here: the sign and the missing second-order term. The modified duration term must be negative, because an expected rise in yields produces an expected fall in price, and the convexity correction is absent. The full expression is E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yields and yield volatility) = (−ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)²].
rationales.B: The coupon rate multiplied by time is a coupon income calculation, not a duration and convexity price-change estimate. It contains neither the modified duration term that captures the linear price-yield response nor the convexity term that corrects for curvature.
rationales.C: E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yields and yield volatility) = (−ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)²]. The modified duration term captures the linear price-yield response and carries a negative sign; the convexity term is the second-order (curvature) correction. For bonds with embedded options, effective duration and effective convexity are used in place of the modified measures. A floating-rate note's modified duration is largely attributable to spread changes rather than to changes in benchmark yields.

questions.stem: A corporate bond portfolio has a modified duration of 3.70 and convexity of 18. If the manager expects the benchmark yield to rise by 0.26% over the horizon, the expected price change based on that yield view is closest to:

rationales.A: −0.26% is only the expected change in yield, not the price impact of it. The yield change has to be scaled by modified duration, 3.70 here, and then corrected for convexity before it becomes a price change.
rationales.B: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong. An expected increase in yields produces an expected decline in price, so the modified duration term is negative: (−3.70 × 0.0026) = −0.00962, which the small positive convexity term barely offsets.
rationales.C: E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yields) = (−ModDur × ΔYield) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔYield)²] = (−3.70 × 0.0026) + [½ × 18 × (0.0026)²] = −0.00962 + 0.0000608 = −0.00956, or approximately −0.96%. The negative sign reflects the expected price decline that follows from the expected yield increase: the manager expects to incur a decrease in prices and a reduction in return based on her rate view. At a yield change this small the convexity contribution is negligible, roughly 0.006 of a percentage point.

questions.stem: An investor's expected bond price change based on a view of yield spreads is most likely:

options.A: A spread change applied on its own.
options.B: A negative spread duration term plus a convexity adjustment.
options.C: A convexity term applied to the level of the spread.

rationales.A: The structural components are missing. A spread change on its own is not a price change: it must be scaled by modified spread duration and then corrected for convexity, giving E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yield spreads) = (−ModSpreadDur × ΔSpread) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²].
rationales.B: E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yield spreads) = (−ModSpreadDur × ΔSpread) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²]. When economic and credit conditions improve, spreads typically tighten (narrow), reducing the required yield and lifting price; deteriorating conditions lead to higher required yields and lower prices. This component reflects general market conditions rather than any spread change due to issuer-specific (idiosyncratic) risk, although credit migration, a change in rating, may also drive the spread on an individual bond.
rationales.C: Convexity multiplied by the level of the spread is not the expression. Convexity enters only as a second-order correction applied to the squared change in the spread, and the first-order term is modified spread duration multiplied by the spread change, carrying a negative sign.

questions.curriculum_ref: A Model for FI Returns — spread-view formula

questions.stem: A corporate bond portfolio has a modified spread duration of 3.70 and convexity of 18. If the manager expects spreads to narrow by 0.10% over the horizon, the expected price change based on that spread view is closest to:

rationales.A: E(ΔPrice based on the investor's views of yield spreads) = (−ModSpreadDur × ΔSpread) + [½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²] = (−3.70 × −0.0010) + [½ × 18 × (−0.0010)²] = +0.0037 + 0.000009 = +0.00371, or approximately +0.37%. The result is positive because a narrowing spread lowers the required yield and therefore lifts the price; applying spread duration to a narrowing spread produces a price gain.
rationales.B: +3.70% is the modified spread duration itself read off as a percentage. It has not been scaled by the 0.10% expected spread change, and the convexity effect is left out as well.
rationales.C: The sign is wrong for narrowing spreads. A spread that narrows reduces the required yield and raises the price, so the expected price impact is positive; a figure of −0.37% would correspond to spreads widening by 0.10% instead.

questions.stem: For a foreign-currency bond position, the domestic-currency return is most likely:

options.A: The foreign-currency and currency returns compounded.
options.B: The foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied.
options.C: The foreign-currency and currency returns summed.

rationales.A: R_DC = (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1 for a single asset, and R_DC = Σ ω_i (1 + R_FC,i)(1 + R_FX,i) − 1 for a portfolio, where R_DC and R_FC are the domestic- and foreign-currency returns as a percentage, R_FX is the percentage change of the foreign currency versus the domestic currency, and ω_i are the portfolio weights. Appreciation of the foreign currency increases the domestic-currency return. The relationship is compound rather than simple, because the currency return applies to the foreign-currency value after that value has already grown by R_FC.
rationales.B: Simple multiplication of the two returns is not the relationship; the returns compound as (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1. The bare product R_FC × R_FX is only the cross-term of that expansion, and on its own it would, for instance, report a positive domestic-currency return when both the bond and the currency lost value.
rationales.C: The sum ignores the cross-term R_FC × R_FX. Adding the two returns is a serviceable approximation only when both are small; compounding as (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) − 1 is the accurate formulation.

questions.curriculum_ref: A Model for FI Returns — currency returns

questions.stem: A manager's expected return decomposition for a bond portfolio shows coupon income of 2.83%, rolldown return of 0.17%, a price change of −0.96% from her yield view, a price change of +0.37% from her spread view, and an expected currency loss of 0.50%. The total expected return is closest to:

rationales.A: 3.00% is the rolling yield only: coupon income of 2.83% plus rolldown return of 0.17%. It ignores the two price-view components and the expected currency loss, and so overstates the total expected return.
rationales.B: Total expected return = coupon income (2.83%) + rolldown return (0.17%) + E(ΔPrice based on the yield view) (−0.96%) + E(ΔPrice based on the spread view) (+0.37%) + expected currency loss (−0.50%) = 1.91%. The rolling yield, coupon income plus rolldown, is 3.00%, but the additional views and the currency loss together subtract 1.09 percentage points and bring the total expected return to 1.91%.
rationales.C: 0.50% is the expected currency loss taken on its own. It is one of five components of the expected return, not the total.

questions.curriculum_ref: A Model for FI Returns — Smith total

questions.stem: A limitation of decomposing the expected return on a fixed-income portfolio is least likely:

options.A: a requirement for perfect forecasts of every input.
options.B: a reliance on duration and convexity as approximations.
options.C: an assumption that cash flows are reinvested at the yield to maturity.

rationales.A: The decomposition does not require perfect forecasts; it simply acknowledges that the yield, spread and currency inputs are its most uncertain components. The limitations actually identified are: (1) the model is an approximation that summarizes the price-yield relationship using only duration and convexity; (2) it implicitly assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the yield to maturity, which gives different coupon reinvestment rates for different bonds; (3) it ignores local richness and cheapness effects, the deviations of individual maturity segments from the fitted yield curve; and (4) it ignores potential financing advantages, such as those available in the repo market. Those local effects are typically small, which is why they are omitted from the decomposition.
rationales.B: This is one of the limitations. Duration and convexity summarize the price-yield relationship only approximately, so the price-view components of the decomposition are estimates rather than exact price changes.
rationales.C: This is one of the limitations. The decomposition implicitly assumes that all intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the yield to maturity, which means different bonds are assumed to reinvest their coupons at different rates.
