drills.los_text: discuss the use of leverage, alternative methods for leveraging, and risks that leverage creates in fixed-income portfolios

questions.stem: The return on a leveraged fixed-income portfolio is most likely:

options.A: The invested return multiplied by the borrowing rate.
options.B: The invested return plus leverage times the spread over the borrowing rate.
options.C: The invested return less the borrowing rate.

rationales.A: Multiplying the invested return by the borrowing rate has no economic meaning. Leverage works by adding a term that depends on how much has been borrowed, not by scaling the invested return up or down by the cost of that borrowing, and the product of two rates is not itself a portfolio return.
rationales.B: The leveraged portfolio return decomposes as r_P = r_I + (V_B / V_E) × (r_I − r_B), where r_P is the leveraged portfolio return, r_I is the return on invested funds, r_B is the borrowing rate, V_B is borrowed funds and V_E is equity. The leveraged return therefore equals the return on invested funds plus a leverage-dependent term. If r_I > r_B, that second term is positive and leverage boosts return; if r_I < r_B, leverage reduces return. The degree of enhancement or drag is proportional to both the leverage ratio (V_B/V_E) and the spread (r_I − r_B).
rationales.C: Simple subtraction omits the leverage multiplier V_B/V_E applied to the spread (r_I − r_B). The spread is earned on borrowed funds only, so it must be scaled by V_B/V_E before being added to r_I; subtracting the borrowing rate from the invested return also charges a full borrowing cost against equity capital that was never borrowed.

questions.stem: The transaction that is least likely to be a method of leveraging a fixed-income portfolio is:

options.A: Cash purchases of bonds without financing.
options.B: Futures contracts and interest rate swaps.
options.C: Repurchase agreements and security lending.

rationales.A: Unlevered cash purchases are the baseline against which leverage is measured, not a method of obtaining it: no funds are borrowed and no notional exposure is taken beyond the equity committed. The four common leveraging methods are (1) futures contracts, which embed significant leverage because a modest margin deposit controls a much larger notional; (2) swap agreements, economically equivalent to long–short bond portfolios and so providing leveraged exposure against only collateral capital; (3) repurchase agreements, or repos, which are collateralized loans; and (4) security lending, where the financing motivation is collateralized by cash or high-credit-quality bonds.
rationales.B: Futures and interest rate swaps are two of the four methods. Futures give exposure to a large quantity of the underlying while requiring only a margin deposit, and a swap is economically equivalent to a long–short bond portfolio funded with collateral alone.
rationales.C: Repurchase agreements and security lending are two of the four methods. A repo is effectively a collateralized loan against the security sold, and security lending supplies financing collateralized by cash or high-credit-quality bonds.

questions.stem: Futures leverage is most likely computed as:

options.A: Notional value in excess of margin, divided by margin.
options.B: Notional value divided by margin.
options.C: Margin divided by notional value.

rationales.A: Futures leverage is the futures exposure in excess of the margin deposit, normalized by the amount of margin required to control the notional amount: (Notional value − Margin) / Margin. Futures contracts embed significant leverage because they permit the counterparties to gain exposure to a large quantity of the underlying asset without transacting in the underlying, so a modest margin deposit controls a much larger notional.
rationales.B: Notional value divided by margin is the total, or gross, exposure ratio: it counts the margin the investor has actually posted as part of the leveraged exposure. The leverage measure nets margin out of the numerator first, so this overstates leverage by exactly one turn.
rationales.C: Margin divided by notional value inverts the relationship. It expresses the margin requirement as a fraction of exposure, a number below one that falls as leverage rises rather than rising with it.

questions.stem: The fixed-rate payer in an interest rate swap is most likely equivalent to being:

options.A: Long a fixed-rate bond and long a floating-rate bond.
options.B: Short a fixed-rate bond and long a floating-rate bond.
options.C: Long a fixed-rate bond and short a floating-rate bond.

rationales.A: A swap exchanges one stream of payments for another, so its economic equivalent must pair a long bond position with a short one. Holding both a fixed-rate and a floating-rate bond long is an unlevered portfolio with no offsetting obligation, and it would gain or lose on both legs rather than on the difference between them.
rationales.B: The fixed-rate payer is effectively short a fixed-rate bond and long a floating-rate bond. When interest rates increase, the value of the swap to the fixed-rate payer increases, because the present value of the fixed-rate liability decreases while the floating-rate payments received increase. Only collateral capital is required to hold the position, which is why a swap provides leveraged exposure.
rationales.C: Long a fixed-rate bond and short a floating-rate bond is the fixed-rate receiver's position, the opposite side of the swap. That position gains if rates decline, as the fixed-rate asset appreciates, whereas the fixed-rate payer gains when rates rise.

questions.stem: A repurchase agreement (repo) is most likely:

options.A: A securities loan on which the lender of the security pays the cash borrower a rebate.
options.B: An unsecured short-term loan priced at the central bank's policy rate.
options.C: A sale of a security with a simultaneous agreement to repurchase it at a set future price.

rationales.A: This confuses a repo with securities lending, a related but distinct transaction. In a repo, the security owner sells the security for cash and repurchases it at a specified future date and price, effectively borrowing at the repo rate rather than receiving a rebate. A rebate rate arises in securities lending, where the lender of the security returns part of the earnings on posted collateral to the borrower.
rationales.B: A repo is collateralized, not unsecured: the security sold, together with the simultaneous agreement to repurchase it, serves as the cash lender's collateral. The repo rate is negotiated transaction by transaction against the quality and term of that collateral rather than set at the central bank's policy rate.
rationales.C: A repurchase agreement is a sale of a security for a specific cash amount with a simultaneous agreement to repurchase that security at a specified future date, typically one day later, and price, which makes it effectively a collateralized loan. Repos are important sources of short-term financing for fixed-income security dealers and other financial institutions, evidenced by trillions of dollars of volume annually. From the borrower's standpoint the transaction is a repo; from the cash lender's standpoint, such as a money market fund, it is a reverse repo.

questions.stem: A dealer finances a €15 million bond position with a 1-day repurchase agreement at a repo rate of 5% on a 360-day basis. The repo interest is closest to:

rationales.A: Dollar interest = Principal × Repo rate × (Term of repo in days / 360) = €15,000,000 × 5% × (1/360) = €15,000,000 × 0.05 × 0.002778 = €2,083.33. The dealer will therefore repurchase the bond the next day for €15,002,083.33. The 360-day convention is the one used for money market and repo calculations.
rationales.B: €1,041.67 is half the correct amount, which follows from halving either the rate or the day count: 2.5% for one day, or 5% for half a day. One day of interest on €15,000,000 at 5% on a 360-day basis is €15,000,000 × 0.05 × (1/360) = €2,083.33.
rationales.C: €10,416.67 is five times the correct amount, which follows from applying a term longer than the single day of the agreement or from misapplying the day-count denominator. The term of this repo is one day, giving €15,000,000 × 0.05 × (1/360) = €2,083.33.

questions.stem: When bonds are posted as collateral in a security lending transaction, the rebate rate is most likely:

options.A: Fixed at zero by market convention.
options.B: Positive however strong borrowing demand becomes.
options.C: The collateral earnings rate less the security lending rate.

rationales.A: The rebate equals the collateral earnings rate minus the security lending rate, so it is normally positive rather than zero: income earned on bond collateral usually exceeds the security lending rate, and the security lender repays part of that interest to the borrower. No convention fixes the rebate at zero.
rationales.B: The rebate is not always positive. For hard-to-borrow securities in extreme demand, typically because there is heavy demand to short them, the rebate rate can turn negative, because the fee for borrowing the securities exceeds the return earned on the collateral.
rationales.C: When bonds are posted as collateral, the income earned on the collateral usually exceeds the security lending rate, so the security lender, which is in possession of the bonds, repays the security borrower a portion of the interest earned on that bond collateral. Rebate rate = Collateral earnings rate − Security lending rate. When securities are difficult to borrow, typically because there is high demand to short them, the rebate rate may be negative: the fee for borrowing the securities exceeds the return on the collateral, and the security borrower pays a fee in addition to forgoing the collateral interest.

questions.stem: A risk of using leverage in a fixed-income portfolio is most likely:

options.A: Forced liquidations as falling portfolio value raises leverage.
options.B: Additional financing extended by counterparties during a crisis.
options.C: Leverage declining automatically as portfolio value falls.

rationales.A: Leverage can lead to forced liquidations. Borrowings do not fall when asset values do, so if portfolio value decreases, equity relative to borrowing is reduced and portfolio leverage increases, potentially requiring portfolio assets to be sold to reduce leverage; a fire sale is such a forced liquidation at prices below fair value. The other leverage risks are the amplification of losses, since a heavily leveraged portfolio can incur significant losses from a moderate valuation decline, and counterparty reassessment of risk in a crisis such as the 2008–09 global financial crisis, when counterparties withdraw credit lines, repos and security lending and force leveraged investors to reduce exposure at the worst possible time.
rationales.B: Crises work the other way. Counterparties reassess counterparty risk and withdraw credit lines, repos and securities lending, forcing leveraged investors to reduce exposure at the worst possible time, rather than extending additional financing to stabilize them.
rationales.C: The reverse occurs. Borrowings are fixed in amount and do not fall with asset values, so a decline in portfolio value reduces equity relative to borrowing and increases leverage, potentially forcing asset sales, or fire sales, at prices below fair value.

questions.stem: A manager of a fully invested global aggregate bond fund expects US Treasury rates to rise and Brazilian interest rates to fall. The manager can most appropriately express both views by:

options.A: Buying additional US Treasuries in the cash market.
options.B: Converting the entire fund to cash.
options.C: Selling US Treasury futures and receiving fixed on a Brazilian rate swap.

rationales.A: Buying additional US Treasuries increases the interest rate exposure that the bearish rate view says should be cut, and it would deepen losses if Treasury rates rise as expected. It also does nothing to express the bullish Brazilian view, and a fully invested fund has no cash with which to do it.
rationales.B: Full liquidation forfeits the bullish Brazilian rate view and abandons the fund's mandate. Derivatives express both views without wholesale portfolio turnover, since only counterparty collateral is required.
rationales.C: Being bearish on US Treasury rates requires reducing duration: sell US Treasury futures whose notional and duration offset enough of the corporate bond duration to reach the new target duration. That sheds interest rate risk while retaining spread duration exposure to the corporates. Being bullish on Brazilian rates calls for entering a receive-fixed, pay-floating swap on Brazilian rates, which effectively creates a long fixed-rate bond position that will appreciate if Brazilian rates fall. Both positions are leveraged, since only counterparty collateral is posted, and an incorrect view on either position magnifies losses, potentially requiring the position to be closed at an inopportune time.

drills.los_text: discuss differences in managing fixed-income portfolios for taxable and tax-exempt investors

questions.stem: A difference between managing fixed-income portfolios for taxable investors and for tax-exempt investors is most likely that:

options.A: Taxable investors should maximize pre-tax yield.
options.B: Tax-exempt investors prefer municipal bonds for their tax-exempt coupons.
options.C: Tax-exempt investors focus on pre-tax risk-adjusted returns.

rationales.A: Managers can influence taxes, for example through the timing of realized gains and losses, so taxes are not outside the manager's control. A prudent taxable investor evaluates decisions on expected and realized after-tax returns rather than on pre-tax yield alone.
rationales.B: The tax exemption on municipal coupons is already priced into their lower yields, so the benefit of the exemption accrues to taxable investors. A tax-exempt investor gains nothing from it and would simply be accepting a lower yield; such an investor focuses instead on the highest available pre-tax risk-adjusted return.
rationales.C: A tax-exempt investor's objective is to achieve the highest possible risk-adjusted return net of fees and transaction costs, measured on a pre-tax basis. A prudent taxable investor needs to also consider the effects of taxes on both expected and realized net investment returns. The industry has traditionally made decisions on pre-tax returns as though investors were tax exempt, like pension funds in many countries, yet most of the world's investable assets are owned by taxable investors, who are concerned with after-tax returns.

questions.stem: A principle common to most tax codes in their treatment of fixed-income investments is least likely:

options.A: Unlimited offset of capital losses against ordinary income.
options.B: A lower effective rate on capital gains than on interest income.
options.C: Coupon income and capital gains as the two primary income sources.

rationales.A: Capital losses generally cannot be used to reduce sources of income other than capital gains, so an unlimited offset against ordinary income is not a feature most tax codes share. Capital losses reduce capital gains in the tax year in which they occur, and if losses exceed gains they can often be carried forward, and in some countries carried back, with limits on the number of years typically applying. The principles most tax codes do have in common are: (1) the two primary sources of investment income are coupon payments (interest income) and capital gains or losses; (2) tax is typically due only on amounts actually received, with exceptions such as imputed interest on zero-coupon bonds; (3) capital gains are frequently taxed at a lower effective rate than interest income; (4) capital losses can be carried forward; and (5) short-term gains are often taxed at a higher rate than long-term gains.
rationales.B: Preferential treatment of capital gains relative to interest income is one of the shared principles. Interest income is generally taxed as ordinary income in the year it is received, whereas a capital gain is taxed only when realized and, where the holding period is long enough, often at a lower statutory rate, so the effective rate on gains is frequently the lower of the two.
rationales.C: Coupon payments (interest income) and capital gains or losses are the two primary sources of investment income from a fixed-income portfolio, which is the first of the principles most tax codes have in common rather than an exception to them.

questions.stem: In some countries, the special tax treatment applied to zero-coupon bonds most likely involves:

options.A: Imputed interest taxed over the bond's life.
options.B: Deferral of all tax until maturity.
options.C: The entire return taxed as a capital gain at issuance.

rationales.A: In general, tax is payable only on capital gains and interest income that have been received. In some countries an exception to that rule applies to zero-coupon bonds: imputed interest, accruing as the bond's price moves toward par, may be calculated and taxed throughout the bond's life. This method of taxation ensures that tax is paid over the life of the bond and that the return on a zero-coupon bond is not taxed entirely as a capital gain.
rationales.B: Deferral of the whole liability to maturity is not the special treatment. In the countries that apply it, imputed interest is calculated and taxed throughout the bond's life precisely so that the return is not deferred and then taxed in one lump as a capital gain.
rationales.C: Nothing is taxed at issuance, when no interest has accrued and no gain has been realized. Where the special treatment applies, imputed interest accrues and is taxed over the holding period, which is the opposite of treating the full return as a single capital gain.

questions.stem: Tax-loss harvesting is most likely:

options.A: Delaying realization of gains and realizing losses as early as possible.
options.B: Realizing gains as early as possible and deferring the realization of losses.
options.C: Selling losing positions and immediately repurchasing them to reset cost basis.

rationales.A: Tax-loss harvesting is tax-driven strategic behavior: delaying the realization of gains and realizing losses as early as possible. An investor generally cannot control when coupon income is received, and so cannot control the timing of tax on interest income, but the investor can decide when to sell an investment and therefore controls the timing of realized capital gains and losses. That control is valuable because it may be optimal to delay realizing gains and the related tax payments, since tax deferral increases the present value of the investment, and to realize losses in order to offset current or future capital gains.
rationales.B: This reverses the strategy. Gains are delayed rather than accelerated, because deferring the tax payment increases the present value of the investment, and losses are realized as early as possible so that they can offset current or future capital gains.
rationales.C: Harvesting realizes losses in order to offset capital gains. Selling a position and immediately buying it back to reset the cost basis is generally restricted by wash-sale-type rules and is not the behavior described: the value comes from the usable loss and from deferring gains, not from a costless basis adjustment.

questions.curriculum_ref: Principles of Fixed-Income Taxation — tax-loss harvesting

questions.stem: In managing a taxable fixed-income portfolio, a recommended practice is least likely:

options.A: Selectively offsetting capital gains and losses for tax purposes.
options.B: Controlling turnover to defer capital gains taxes.
options.C: Maximizing turnover to increase active management alpha.

rationales.A: Selectively offsetting capital gains and losses for tax purposes is one of the key points in managing a taxable fixed-income portfolio. It is paired with being judicious when realizing short-term gains, since short-term rates are often higher than long-term rates.
rationales.B: Controlling turnover is one of the key points: lower turnover allows capital gains tax payments to be deferred longer, and it works alongside realizing losses while considering their tax consequences so that those losses offset current or future gains.
rationales.C: Maximizing turnover is the opposite of what is recommended. Lower turnover allows capital gains tax payments to be deferred longer, and that deferral raises the present value of after-tax wealth, so turnover is to be controlled rather than maximized. The five key points for managing a taxable fixed-income portfolio are: (1) selectively offset capital gains and losses for tax purposes; (2) be judicious when realizing short-term gains if short-term rates are higher; (3) realize losses considering tax consequences, so as to offset current or future gains; (4) control turnover, since lower turnover means a longer deferral of capital gains tax; and (5) consider the trade-off between capital gains and income for tax purposes.

questions.curriculum_ref: Key Points for Managing Taxable Portfolios

questions.stem: In pooled investment vehicles like mutual funds, interest income is most likely:

options.A: Taxed at the investor level in the year it arises.
options.B: Taxed only at termination of the fund.
options.C: Never taxed to the investor.

rationales.A: In a pooled investment vehicle, or collective investment scheme, such as a mutual fund, interest income is generally taxed at the final investor level when it occurs, regardless of whether the fund reinvests the interest income or pays it out to investors. For tax purposes the fund is considered to have distributed the interest income in the year it is received even if it does not actually pay it out, so reinvestment inside the fund does not postpone the investor's tax.
rationales.B: Termination of the fund is not the taxing point for interest income. The income is attributed to the investor in the year the fund receives it, whether or not any cash is distributed at that time.
rationales.C: Interest income is not exempt at the investor level. It is taxed to the final investor in the year it arises inside the fund, which is precisely why holding the bonds through a pooled vehicle rather than directly does not shelter the coupon income.

questions.stem: Pass-through treatment of capital gains realized inside a mutual fund is most likely:

options.A: Used in no jurisdiction.
options.B: Used in every jurisdiction.
options.C: Used in the United States but not in the United Kingdom.

rationales.A: Pass-through treatment does exist. The United States applies it: realized net capital gains in the underlying securities of a fund are treated as if distributed to investors in the year they arise, so those gains go on the investor's tax return then rather than being deferred until the fund shares are sold.
rationales.B: Treatment is not uniform across jurisdictions. The United Kingdom, for example, does not use pass-through treatment: realized gains inside the fund increase the fund's net asset value, and the investor pays tax on the net capital gain only on selling the fund shares.
rationales.C: Some countries, such as the United States, use pass-through treatment of capital gains in mutual funds. Realized net capital gains in the underlying securities of a fund are treated as if distributed to investors in the year that they arise, and investors need to include those gains on their tax returns. Other countries, such as the United Kingdom, do not use pass-through treatment: realized capital gains within a fund increase the net asset value of the fund shares, and investors pay tax on the net capital gain when they sell those shares, which defers the capital gains tax payment. One consequence is that a UK portfolio manager's decisions about when to realize gains and losses do not affect the timing of investors' tax payments.

questions.stem: In a separately managed account (SMA), the investor most likely:

options.A: Pays tax as if the account were a pooled vehicle.
options.B: Pays tax on realized gains in the underlying securities as they occur.
options.C: Pays no tax until the account is closed.

rationales.A: A separately managed account is distinct from a pooled vehicle for tax purposes. The investor holds the underlying securities directly rather than holding shares in a fund, so the tax follows realized gains and losses on those individual securities instead of fund-level attribution or distribution rules.
rationales.B: In a separately managed account an investor typically pays tax on realized gains in the underlying securities at the time they occur, because the investor holds the securities directly rather than through shares in a fund. The portfolio manager therefore needs to consider the tax consequences for the investor when making investment decisions. Tax-loss harvesting is particularly valuable in this structure, since the manager can directly manage the timing of realized gains and losses for each client.
rationales.C: Closing the account is not the taxing point. Every sale of an individual security held in the account is a taxable event for the investor at the time it occurs, which is why the manager must weigh tax consequences trade by trade.

questions.stem: Asset-driven liabilities (ADL), compared with liability-driven investing (LDI), is most likely the approach that:

options.A: is the more common of the two in practice.
options.B: takes the assets as given and structures the liabilities to manage interest rate risk.
options.C: takes the liabilities as given and structures the assets to manage interest rate risk.

rationales.A: LDI is much more common than ADL. Liability-driven investing covers the typical institutional cases: a life insurer investing against liabilities created by the policies it has underwritten, or a defined benefit pension plan investing against future employee benefits. ADL is the less common case, such as a leasing company with short-term lease contracts that finances itself with short-term debt so that asset and liability maturities match.
rationales.B: LDI and ADL are both special cases of asset/liability management, and the key difference is which side is given. With ADL the assets are given and the liabilities are structured to manage interest rate risk, as with a leasing company holding short-term lease assets that issues maturity-matched short-term debt. With LDI, which is much more common, the liabilities are given and the assets are managed.
rationales.C: This reverses the direction. Liabilities given with the assets managed describes LDI, the much more common case, as with a life insurer's underwritten policies or a defined benefit plan's future employee benefits. Under ADL the assets are given and the liabilities are structured to manage interest rate risk.

questions.stem: For a manufacturing company whose operating revenues are highly correlated with the business cycle and where monetary policy positively correlates interest rates with the business cycle, the ADL preference is most likely for:

options.A: No liabilities at all.
options.B: Variable-rate liabilities.
options.C: Fixed-rate liabilities.

rationales.A: Carrying no liabilities is not the choice at issue; the company needs financing, and the question is whether that financing should carry a variable or a fixed rate given how its revenues move.
rationales.B: A manufacturing company might identify that its operating revenues are highly correlated with the business cycle. Monetary policy is typically managed so that there is positive correlation between interest rates and the business cycle, because central banks lower policy rates when the economy is weak and raise them when it is strong. This company therefore has a natural preference for variable-rate liabilities, so that operating revenue and interest expense rise and fall together and the interest burden is lightest when revenues are weakest.
rationales.C: Fixed-rate liabilities would hold interest expense flat while operating revenue moved with the business cycle, so the financing cost would be countercyclical to revenue and would weigh most heavily in a downturn, the opposite of what this revenue profile calls for.

questions.stem: In the classification of liabilities by the amount and the timing of the cash outlay, a Type I liability most likely has:

options.A: Known amount and known timing.
options.B: Uncertain amount and uncertain timing.
options.C: Known amount but uncertain timing.

rationales.A: A Type I liability has both a known amount and known timing of cash outlay. The standard example is a traditional fixed-income bond with no embedded options, and its interest rate sensitivity can be measured with Macaulay duration, modified duration, money duration, and PVBP. The full classification by amount and timing runs: Type I, known amount and known timing; Type II, known amount and uncertain timing; Type III, uncertain amount and known timing; Type IV, uncertain amount and uncertain timing.
rationales.B: Uncertain in both amount and timing describes a Type IV liability, such as a property and casualty insurer's exposure to losses whose size and date are both unknown, or a defined benefit plan's payments to current employees. A Type I liability is certain on both dimensions.
rationales.C: A known amount with uncertain timing describes a Type II liability, such as a callable bond whose payment amount is fixed but whose redemption date depends on whether the issuer calls it. A Type I liability has known timing as well as a known amount.

questions.stem: A callable bond is most likely a:

options.A: Type IV liability.
options.B: Type I liability.
options.C: Type II liability.

rationales.A: The amount owed on a callable bond is known, so only one of the two dimensions is in doubt. Type IV requires that both the amount and the timing of the cash outlays be uncertain, which does not describe a callable bond.
rationales.B: The issuer's call option makes the timing of principal repayment uncertain, because the principal may be repaid at a call date rather than at final maturity. Type I requires both the amount and the timing of cash outlays to be known with certainty, so a callable bond cannot be Type I.
rationales.C: Type II liabilities have a known amount but uncertain timing. Callable and putable bonds are the standard examples: the embedded option means principal may be repaid before final maturity, so the payment date cannot be fixed in advance even though the amount is defined. A term life insurance policy is the same type, since the timing of death is unknown but the payout amount is set by the contract. Because the cash flows are not fixed, effective duration is the appropriate measure of interest rate sensitivity for Type II, III, and IV liabilities.

questions.stem: A floating-rate note is most likely a:

options.A: Type IV liability.
options.B: Type I liability.
options.C: Type III liability.

rationales.A: Type IV liabilities have both the amount and the timing uncertain. A floating-rate note's payment dates are fixed by its schedule, so the timing is known and only the amount is in doubt.
rationales.B: Type I liabilities have cash flows known with certainty in both amount and timing. A floater's coupon amounts are not known in advance, because each one is set from the reference rate at the reset date.
rationales.C: Type III liabilities have an uncertain amount but known timing. A floating-rate note is the standard example: the payment dates are set by the note's schedule, but the interest payments depend on future interest rates and are not known until the reset dates. Inflation-protected securities are also Type III, because the amounts of both the interest and the principal payments depend on inflation while the payment dates remain fixed.

questions.stem: Property and casualty insurance liabilities are most likely classified as:

options.A: Type III liabilities.
options.B: Type IV liabilities.
options.C: Type II liabilities.

rationales.A: Type III pairs an uncertain amount with known timing, and the timing half fails here. Property and casualty losses cannot be scheduled, because the occurrence date of a weather event is unpredictable.
rationales.B: Type IV liabilities have both an uncertain amount and uncertain timing, and property and casualty insurance is the standard example: weather events are difficult to predict, so neither the loss amount nor the date of occurrence is known until the event happens. For Type II, III, and IV liabilities, effective duration is needed. It is computed using a model for the uncertain cash flows together with an initial assumption about the yield curve; the curve is then shifted up and down to obtain new present value estimates from which the duration is derived.
rationales.C: Weather-driven losses make the amount uncertain as well as the timing, since the size of a claim is not known until the loss is settled. Type II requires a known amount with only the timing in doubt.

questions.stem: Residential mortgage loans held by a savings bank, on which the homeowner holds a prepayment option, are most likely:

options.A: Type I assets.
options.B: Type III assets.
options.C: Type IV assets.

rationales.A: The homeowner's prepayment option is a call option, and it destroys the certainty of timing that Type I requires: principal can arrive at any point before the scheduled maturity of the loan.
rationales.B: Timing is the uncertain element here, which is what rules out Type III. Type III pairs an uncertain amount with known timing, whereas prepayments arrive unpredictably, placing the mortgages in Type IV.
rationales.C: Residential mortgage loans are Type IV assets to the savings bank. The timing of the interest and principal cash flows is uncertain because of the prepayment option held by the homeowner, which is a complex call option. Homeowners might prepay for many reasons, such as sale of the property or a refinancing if rates decline, so a prepayment model is needed to project the timing. Default risk also affects the projected amount of the cash flows: even if the average loan-to-value ratio is a high-quality 80%, some loans could carry higher LTVs and be more subject to default, especially if home prices decline.

questions.stem: Liability-based fixed-income mandates most likely include:

options.A: Cash flow matching and contingent immunization, but not duration matching.
options.B: Cash flow matching, duration matching, and contingent immunization.
options.C: Duration matching, understood as matching each liability payout with a bond cash flow.

rationales.A: Duration matching is itself a liability-based immunization approach, not a total return mandate. Total return mandates are benchmarked to bond market indexes rather than to a liability stream, and that is the distinction separating the two families of mandates, so excluding duration matching from the liability-based group is wrong.
rationales.B: Liability-based mandates comprise three approaches. Cash flow matching is an immunization approach that attempts to ensure all future liability payouts are matched precisely by cash flows from bonds or fixed-income derivatives. Duration matching is an immunization approach based on the duration of assets and liabilities: ideally, both the liability portfolio and the bond portfolio are affected similarly by a change in interest rates. Contingent immunization is a hybrid approach that combines immunization with active management when assets exceed the present value of the liabilities. Any of the three may be implemented using derivatives overlays.
rationales.C: Matching every liability payout precisely with asset cash flows describes cash flow matching, not duration matching. Duration matching instead aligns the duration, that is the interest rate sensitivity, of the assets and the liabilities so that both respond similarly to a change in rates. It is also only one of the three liability-based approaches rather than the whole category.

drills.los_text: describe the strategy of cash flow matching

questions.stem: Cash flow matching is best described as:

options.A: Hedging duration risk with derivatives while disregarding cash flow timing.
options.B: Rolling over short-term bills continuously to fund liabilities as they fall due.
options.C: Holding a dedicated portfolio of high-quality bonds matched to scheduled outflows.

rationales.A: Hedging duration risk with derivatives is a different technique. Cash flow matching works by aligning the actual cash flows of the bonds held with each liability payment, so the timing of those cash flows is central to it rather than something set aside.
rationales.B: A rolling program of short-term bills is not the approach described. Cash flow matching builds a dedicated portfolio whose cash flows match both the amount and the timing of the scheduled payouts, rather than relying on repeated reinvestment at unknown future short-term rates.
rationales.C: Cash flow matching is a classic strategy for eliminating the interest rate risk arising from multiple liabilities. It builds a dedicated asset portfolio of high-quality fixed-income bonds that, as closely as possible, matches the amount and the timing of the scheduled cash outflows. The word dedicated means the bonds are placed in a held-to-maturity portfolio, so the match between asset cash flows and liability payouts is not disturbed by trading.

questions.stem: Relative to repurchasing its outstanding debt, a corporation's motivation for cash flow matching is most likely:

options.A: The cost of buying back bonds widely held by buy-and-hold investors.
options.B: A regulatory prohibition on repurchasing bonds.
options.C: A lower cost than any available repurchase.

rationales.A: The natural question is why a corporation holding cash does not simply buy back and retire the liabilities. The buyback strategy is difficult and costly to implement if the bonds are widely held by buy-and-hold institutional and retail investors. Most corporate bonds are rather illiquid, so buying them back on the open market is likely to drive up the purchase price, which makes cash flow matching a better use of the available cash. Cash flow matching can also improve the credit rating, and under some circumstances it allows the corporation to remove both the dedicated assets and the debt liabilities from its balance sheet through accounting defeasance, also called in-substance defeasance. That is a way of extinguishing a debt obligation by setting aside sufficient high-quality securities, such as US Treasury notes, to repay the liability.
rationales.B: No prohibition is at work. Buying back one's own bonds is permitted; the obstacle is practical, in that bonds held by buy-and-hold investors are illiquid and expensive to reacquire on the open market.
rationales.C: The reasoning is structural rather than a general statement about cost. The problem is that illiquid, widely held bonds cannot be reacquired at a reasonable price; where a repurchase could be executed cheaply it would not be ruled out, so a blanket claim that cash flow matching is cheaper than any repurchase is not the motivation.

questions.stem: In cash flow matching, the cash-in-advance constraint most likely means that:

options.A: Securities may be sold freely to meet obligations.
options.B: Cash may not be held at all.
options.C: Securities are not sold to meet obligations.

rationales.A: The constraint is precisely that securities are not sold to meet obligations. The funds must already be on hand, from maturing principal and from coupons received on or before the payment date, so free selling is the opposite of what the constraint allows.
rationales.B: Cash holdings arise naturally between payment dates and are not forbidden. They are in fact a consequence of the constraint rather than something it rules out, and managing them is the problem the constraint creates.
rationales.C: The cash-in-advance constraint means securities are not sold to meet obligations; instead, sufficient funds must be available on or before each liability payment date to meet the obligation. The design of traditional bonds, with a fixed coupon rate and principal redeemed at maturity, is a problem if the liability stream is a level payment annuity. It can lead to large cash holdings between payment dates and therefore to cash flow reinvestment risk, especially if yields on high-quality short-term investments are low or negative.

questions.stem: A borrower must defease debt payments of SEK3.71 million, SEK6.62 million, SEK4.41 million, and SEK5.25 million, due each June from Year 2 through Year 5. Cash flow matching that schedule with government bonds is most likely accomplished by:

options.A: Buying whatever bonds are available, since maturity does not matter.
options.B: Buying a single five-year zero-coupon bond sized to the total obligation.
options.C: Buying bonds backward from the last liability, netting later coupons against earlier par amounts.

rationales.A: Maturity selection is the essence of the strategy. The portfolio is built by working backward from the last liability, matching a bond's final maturity plus its coupons to each obligation in turn, so bonds cannot be chosen without regard to when they mature.
rationales.B: A single zero-coupon bond maturing in Year 5 pays nothing before maturity, so it leaves the Year 2, Year 3, and Year 4 payments unfunded. Each liability date needs matched cash flow arriving on or before that date.
rationales.C: The cash flow matching portfolio is built by starting with the last liability and working backward. For each liability, the required par value of a bond maturing near that date is computed, subtracting the coupons already contributed by the longer-maturity bonds bought earlier in the process. For the Year 5 liability of SEK5.25 million, about SEK4.98 million par of the 5.50% May Year 5 bond is purchased, which yields SEK5,253,900 at maturity. The coupons from that bond flow into the earlier years and reduce the par values required of the shorter-maturity bonds. The final holdings are SEK2.96 million of the 2.75% Year 2 bond, SEK5.95 million of the 3.50% Year 3 bond, SEK3.95 million of the 4.75% Year 4 bond, and SEK4.98 million of the 5.50% Year 5 bond.

questions.stem: A laddered bond portfolio is most likely classified as:

options.A: A technique unrelated to cash flow matching.
options.B: A cash flow matching technique.
options.C: A duration matching technique.

rationales.A: The laddered structure is not outside the cash flow matching family. Its maturing principal is scheduled against the liability payouts, which is the defining feature of cash flow matching, so the two are closely related rather than unrelated.
rationales.B: The so-called laddered portfolio falls into the cash flow matching category of approaches to managing multiple liabilities. Bonds are held across a sequence of maturity dates so that principal returns on a regular schedule and can be applied to liability payouts as they come due. This is distinct from duration matching, which extends the ideas of immunization to a portfolio of debt liabilities by aligning the interest rate sensitivity of assets and liabilities rather than the individual cash flows.
rationales.C: Duration matching is a separate technique, which aligns the interest rate sensitivity of the assets with that of the liabilities. The laddered portfolio instead schedules maturing principal against the liability payments, which places it in the cash flow matching category.

questions.stem: Duration matching — an alternative multi-liability approach — differs from cash flow matching most likely in that:

options.A: it extends immunization ideas to a portfolio of debt liabilities.
options.B: it cannot handle multiple liabilities.
options.C: it precisely matches every cash flow.

rationales.A: Duration matching extends immunization ideas to a portfolio of debt liabilities. Rather than exactly matching each cash flow, duration matching aligns the duration of the asset portfolio with the duration of the liability portfolio, so that the value of the assets and the value of the liabilities are similarly affected by a change in interest rates. That provides interest rate immunization on a portfolio basis rather than liability by liability.
rationales.B: Duration matching does handle multiple liabilities; extending immunization to a portfolio of debt liabilities is the whole point of the approach. What it gives up is exactness at the level of the individual liability: the match is made on portfolio duration, not on each dated obligation.
rationales.C: Precisely matching every cash flow describes cash flow matching, not duration matching. Under cash flow matching, the asset cash flows are dedicated so that each liability is retired by coupon and principal receipts arriving on or before its date. Duration matching instead aligns the duration statistics of assets and liabilities, accepting cash flow mismatches within the horizon.

questions.stem: The convexity of an immunized bond portfolio is most likely a function of:

options.A: cash flow dispersion alone.
options.B: portfolio duration alone.
options.C: duration, cash flow dispersion, and cash flow yield.

rationales.A: Dispersion alone omits the duration terms. Immunized portfolio convexity = [MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion] / (1 + Cash flow yield)², and MacDur² + MacDur is the dominant part of the numerator; dispersion only adds to it.
rationales.B: Duration alone is missing the dispersion term in the numerator and the (1 + Cash flow yield)² denominator. Both appear in Immunized portfolio convexity = [MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion] / (1 + Cash flow yield)², and it is precisely the dispersion term that distinguishes portfolios built to the same duration.
rationales.C: Immunized portfolio convexity = [MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion] / (1 + Cash flow yield)², so it depends on Macaulay duration, the dispersion of the cash flows, and the cash flow yield. Higher cash flow dispersion leads to higher convexity, which is a key property of laddered portfolios. If three portfolios (laddered, bullet, barbell) have the same duration and the same cash flow yield, the barbell has the highest convexity because its dispersion is widest, the bullet has the lowest because its dispersion is tightest, and the laddered portfolio lies in between.

questions.stem: A cash flow matching portfolio must fund a SEK6,158,475 liability due in June of Year 3, and the coupon and principal received in May of that year total SEK6,158,250. The small shortfall is most likely addressed by:

options.A: reinvesting the May cash flows until the June liability date.
options.B: borrowing on the liability date.
options.C: abandoning the strategy.

rationales.A: The May-payment and June-liability timing leaves a short reinvestment window. The shortfall of SEK225 (SEK6,158,475 needed less SEK6,158,250 received) is made up because the funds received in May are reinvested until June. More generally, excess cash in some periods can be held in a bank account to cover shortfalls in others. This illustrates that cash flow matching works in practice even though rounding and minimum-denomination constraints on the bonds purchased make an exact match impossible.
rationales.B: Additional borrowing would break the funded structure. A cash flow matching (defeasance) portfolio is built so that the assets already held retire the liabilities; borrowing at the liability date reintroduces an obligation the strategy exists to extinguish. It is also unnecessary, because a few weeks of reinvestment income on SEK6.16 million covers a gap of SEK225.
rationales.C: The small shortfalls are managed within the strategy, not a reason to abandon it. Because bonds can only be bought in minimum denominations, a dedicated portfolio will almost always leave gaps of a few hundred krona in some periods and excesses in others; reinvesting earlier receipts until the liability date, and holding period excesses in a bank account, absorbs them.

drills.los_text: describe construction, benefits, limitations, and risk–return characteristics of a laddered bond portfolio

questions.stem: A laddered portfolio is most likely:

options.A: concentrated at the short-term and long-term ends of the yield curve.
options.B: concentrated at a single point on the yield curve.
options.C: spread evenly along the yield curve by maturity and par value.

rationales.A: Concentrating bonds at the short-term and long-term ends of the curve describes a barbell portfolio, not a ladder. The barbell holds very short and very long maturities with little in between, which gives it the widest cash flow dispersion of the three structures and therefore the highest convexity for a given duration, but it also leaves the investor with significant reinvestment risk as the short bonds mature.
rationales.B: Concentrating the bonds' maturities at a particular point on the yield curve describes a bullet portfolio, not a ladder. The bullet has the tightest cash flow dispersion of the three structures and therefore the lowest convexity for a given portfolio duration.
rationales.C: A laddered portfolio spreads the bonds' maturities and par values evenly along the yield curve. It is contrasted with a bullet portfolio, which concentrates the bonds at a particular point on the yield curve, and a barbell portfolio, which places the bonds at the short-term and long-term ends of the curve. In principle each of the three can have the same portfolio duration statistic and approximately the same change in value for a parallel shift in the yield curve, but non-parallel shifts and twists produce very different outcomes for the bullet and barbell structures.

questions.stem: An advantage of the laddered portfolio is most likely:

options.A: protection from shifts and twists in the yield curve.
options.B: the highest convexity among duration-matched structures.
options.C: elimination of cash flow reinvestment risk.

rationales.A: An obvious advantage of the laddered portfolio is protection from shifts and twists in the yield curve, because the cash flows are essentially diversified across the time spectrum. That diversification over time gives the investor a balanced position between the two sources of interest rate risk, cash flow reinvestment and market price volatility. Bonds mature each year and the proceeds are reinvested at the longer-term end of the ladder, typically at higher rates, and reinvesting in this way maintains the duration of the overall portfolio.
rationales.B: For a given portfolio duration, the barbell has the highest convexity, because its cash flows have the widest dispersion. A ladder's convexity is relatively high, since its cash flows are spread over the timeline by design, but it sits between the bullet's and the barbell's rather than above both.
rationales.C: Reinvestment risk is balanced, not eliminated. Each maturing rung must still be reinvested at whatever rate prevails at the long end of the ladder when it matures. What the structure achieves is a balance between cash flow reinvestment risk and market price volatility, so that a rate move helps on one side roughly as much as it hurts on the other; neither source of interest rate risk is removed.

questions.stem: For laddered, bullet, and barbell portfolios with the same duration and the same cash flow yield, convexity is most likely:

options.A: highest for the bullet and lowest for the barbell.
options.B: identical across the three portfolios.
options.C: highest for the barbell and lowest for the bullet.

rationales.A: This reverses the correct ordering. Convexity rises with the dispersion of the cash flows, and the bullet has the tightest dispersion while the barbell has the widest, so the bullet has the lowest convexity of the three and the barbell the highest.
rationales.B: Convexity differs across the three even when duration and cash flow yield are held equal. Immunized portfolio convexity = [MacDur² + MacDur + Dispersion] / (1 + Cash flow yield)², so with the duration and yield terms fixed, the dispersion term alone separates the structures.
rationales.C: If the three portfolios have the same duration and the same cash flow yield, the barbell clearly has the highest convexity because its dispersion is widest, and the bullet the lowest because its dispersion is tightest. The laddered portfolio tends to have relatively high convexity, since its cash flows are by design spread over the timeline. Compared with the barbell, however, the laddered portfolio carries much less cash flow reinvestment risk: the barbell is built from very short and very long bonds, so large amounts come due early and must be reinvested at unknown rates.

questions.stem: Perhaps the most desirable aspect of the laddered portfolio in practice is most likely:

options.A: guaranteed reinvestment of maturing rungs at higher rates.
options.B: maximum convexity relative to a duration-matched barbell.
options.C: liquidity management.

rationales.A: Maturing proceeds are typically reinvested at the back of the ladder, often at higher rates when the yield curve slopes upward, but future reinvestment rates are never guaranteed. The ladder balances reinvestment risk against market price volatility rather than removing the uncertainty from either.
rationales.B: A duration-matched barbell has higher convexity than a ladder, because the barbell's cash flows are more widely dispersed. The ladder's convexity is relatively high, lying between the bullet's and the barbell's, so convexity maximization is not what makes the structure attractive in practice.
rationales.C: In practice, perhaps the most desirable aspect of the laddered portfolio is liquidity management. This is particularly relevant if the bonds are not actively traded, as is the case for many corporate securities. As time passes, there is always a bond that is close to redemption; its duration will be low, so its price is fairly stable even in a time of interest rate volatility. If the client needs immediate cash, the soon-to-mature bond makes high-quality collateral for a personal loan or, for an institution, a repo contract. As the bonds mature, the final coupon and principal can be deployed for consumption or reinvested in a long-term bond at the back of the ladder.

questions.stem: A wealth manager building a laddered portfolio for a client would most likely use:

options.A: individual Treasury bills rolled at each maturity.
options.B: equity ETFs spanning multiple sectors.
options.C: fixed-maturity corporate bond ETFs.

rationales.A: Treasury bills all cluster at the short end of the yield curve, so rolling them as they mature produces a money market position rather than maturities and par values spread evenly along the curve. A ladder needs rungs further out, and fixed-maturity corporate bond ETFs, such as a 2029 investment-grade fund, supply them.
rationales.B: Equity funds have no maturity dates, so they provide no rungs; diversifying across sectors does not create the schedule of redemptions on which a ladder depends. It is fixed-maturity bond ETFs that work as the vehicle, because each one has a designated year of maturity.
rationales.C: Another way for a wealth manager to build a laddered portfolio for a client is to use fixed-maturity corporate bond exchange-traded funds (ETFs). These ETFs have a designated year of maturity and credit risk profile, for instance 2029 investment-grade corporate bonds. The passively managed, low-cost ETF seeks to replicate the performance of an index of held-to-maturity investment-grade corporate bonds that mature in that year. Roughly equal positions in a series of such funds, say 2022 through 2029, create a laddered portfolio that should provide the same benefits as holding the bonds directly: price stability in the soonest-to-mature ETF and greater convexity than a bullet portfolio. The ETFs should also be more liquid than positions in the actual bonds.

questions.stem: A limitation of the laddered portfolio approach is most likely that:

options.A: it forgoes the liquidity benefit of holding soon-to-mature bonds.
options.B: it diversifies default risk less well than a fixed-income mutual fund.
options.C: it has lower convexity than a duration-matched bullet portfolio.

rationales.A: The opposite is true: a ladder always holds a bond close to redemption, and that is precisely its liquidity-management advantage. The near-maturity bond has low duration, so its price is fairly stable even in a time of interest rate volatility, it makes high-quality collateral for a personal loan or a repo contract, and its final coupon and principal arrive as cash for consumption or reinvestment.
rationales.B: Laddered portfolios are not without limitations. For many investors, the decision to build a laddered bond portfolio should be weighed against buying shares in a fixed-income mutual fund, especially if the portfolio consists of a limited number of corporate bonds. The mutual fund clearly provides greater diversification of default risk. Moreover, actual bonds can entail a much higher cost of acquisition, and if the entire investment needs to be liquidated, the mutual fund shares can be redeemed more quickly than the bonds can be sold, and likely at a better price.
rationales.C: The comparison is reversed. A ladder's cash flows are spread along the timeline, so its dispersion, and therefore its convexity, is higher than that of a duration-matched bullet, whose cash flows are tightly clustered at one point. Higher convexity is an attraction of the structure rather than a limitation of it.

questions.stem: A laddered portfolio of CNY government bonds holds CNY10 million par maturing in each of 2022, 2024, 2026, and 2029. The key characteristic of a portfolio built this way is most likely:

options.A: concentration of cash flows at the final maturity.
options.B: the highest attainable yield to maturity.
options.C: cash flow diversification across the timeline.

rationales.A: The ladder does the opposite of concentrating cash flows. Because CNY10 million of par matures in each of 2022, 2024, 2026, and 2029, coupon and principal payments arrive throughout the horizon rather than at a single point; concentration at one maturity describes a bullet portfolio.
rationales.B: A laddered portfolio does not maximize yield to maturity. Spreading maturities evenly along the curve trades yield for diversification over time, which balances cash flow reinvestment risk against market price volatility; a portfolio built purely for yield would concentrate wherever the curve paid most.
rationales.C: The laddered portfolio provides cash flow diversification across the timeline, with CNY10 million of par maturing in each of 2022, 2024, 2026, and 2029 on top of the coupons, so the schedule delivers regular known cash flows to the client family. That matters here because most family assets are in residential property and equity and the family relies on regular cash flows. On a total market value of CNY41,143,508 the portfolio has a cash flow yield of 2.661%, higher than the market-value-weighted average yield of 2.455%, and the thirty receipts of coupon and principal are spread across the horizon rather than clustered.
